fire-primitive.works: These ways use what you find around you, so they help when you have no matches or lighter. Flint and steel is the easiest of them.
fire-primitive.reliability: They take time to make and need more energy, patience and skill than modern fire-starters; people who practised them before are much more likely to succeed. The bow drill needs much preparation; the hand drill needs less, but is harder to use for some people.
fire-primitive.mistakes: Using stainless steel instead of carbon steel. Using resinous wood for the drill or the fireboard: it glazes over and hinders the process. Not having enough dry tinder ready when the coal appears.

shelter-site.title: Where to put a shelter

steps.1: When you know you need shelter, start looking for a site as soon as possible. A good site has enough material for the shelter you need and is large enough and level enough for you to lie down and keep your things.

items.1: protects you from sun, wind, rain and snow;
items.2: is free of dead trees that may fall;
items.3: is away from avalanches, rockslides and mudslides, and from places that flash floods or high water reach;
items.4: is free of insects and reptiles;
items.5: is not a low spot where cold air collects;
items.6: lets you signal and be found.

steps.3: Ask yourself: how much time and effort will the shelter need; will it protect you from the weather; do you have the tools and materials; how long will you stay here?
steps.4: Prepare the site: brush away rocks and twigs from where you will sleep, cut back overhanging plants, and look for loose rocks and dead branches that could fall on the shelter. Check the site for snakes, ticks and stinging ants.
steps.5: When you have little time, material or tools, use what is already there (see the picture): caves, rocky crevices, small depressions, large rocks on the side of a hill away from the wind, clumps of bushes, large trees with low-hanging branches, fallen trees with thick branches, the roots of an uprooted tree.
steps.6: A quick shelter can also be a wall or a building, a vehicle, a tarp, a poncho, a piece of plastic or a space blanket — anything that gives cover from above.

shelter-site.works: A shelter protects you from sun, insects, wind, rain, snow, heat and cold. In some areas your need for shelter may come before your need for food, and possibly even your need for water: long exposure to cold can cause great fatigue and weakness.
shelter-site.reliability: Using what is already there saves time, energy and materials; but whatever its kind, a shelter must give the protection you need. Shelters of natural materials usually take the most time and energy to build.
shelter-site.mistakes: Settling under dead trees, or where avalanches, rockslides or floods can reach you. Choosing thick, brushy, low ground: it harbours more insects. Making a fire in or near a vehicle used as a shelter: spilled fuel or oil can catch fire.

shelter-tarp.title: A shelter from a poncho or tarp

steps.1: You need: a poncho or tarp, 7 to 10 feet (2.1⁠–⁠3.0 m) of rope or cord, three stakes about 1 foot (30 cm) long, and two trees or two poles 7 to 10 feet (2.1⁠–⁠3.0 m) apart.
steps.2: Check the wind direction: the back of the lean-to must face into the wind (see the picture).
steps.3: If the poncho has a hood, pull its drawstring tight, roll the hood up, fold it and tie it off with the drawstring. Cut the rope in half and tie one half to each corner grommet of one long side.
steps.4: Tie a short stick — a drip stick, about 4 inches (10 cm) long — to each rope about 1 inch (2.5 cm) from the grommet: rainwater then does not run down the ropes into the shelter.
steps.5: Tie the ropes to the trees about waist high, with a round turn and two half hitches with a quick-release knot.
steps.6: Spread the poncho and anchor it to the ground with sharpened sticks through the grommets.
steps.7: If you will stay more than one night or rain is expected, support the middle: a line from the hood to an overhanging branch, without slack — or a stick upright under the middle, though it takes up space.
steps.8: Put brush or your rucksack at the sides against wind and rain, and leaves or pine needles inside against the cold of the ground.
steps.9: Material without grommets, such as plastic: put a small “button” — a pinch of dirt, an acorn or the like — behind the material, gather the material around it and put a line with a slip loop over the bulge. Then stake the material out and pull out the wrinkles.
steps.10: Stakes: sharpen sticks about 1 inch (2.5 cm) thick and 12 inches (30 cm) long and drive them in at about a 45-degree angle, slanted away from the pull. On rocky or frozen ground, tie the cover to a heavy branch or rock lying on the ground; in loose sand or soil, tie it to a piece of wood or a rock and bury it.

shelter-tarp.works: It takes only a short time and little equipment to build. Material stretched tight at a pitch of 40 to 60 degrees sheds rain and snow.
shelter-tarp.reliability: Porous material, such as parachute cloth, sheds water only when stretched tight at a steep enough angle. At rest, you can lose as much as 80 percent of your body heat to the ground: put insulation under you (card “Bedding and warmth in a shelter”).
shelter-tarp.mistakes: Touching the material while water runs over it: water then drips in at that spot. Leaving it slack or wrinkled: water pools in the wrinkles and leaks in. Turning the open side of the lean-to into the wind.

shelter-debris-hut.title: A hut of branches and leaves

steps.1: Make a frame: a tripod of two short stakes and a long ridgepole — or rest one end of the long ridgepole on a sturdy base, or tie it to a tree at about waist height.
steps.2: Prop large sticks along both sides of the ridgepole, like ribs, in a wedge shape: wide enough for your body and steep enough to shed water.
steps.3: Lay finer sticks and brush crosswise on the ribs: a lattice that keeps the insulating material from falling through into the sleeping space.
steps.4: Pile light, dry, soft debris — grass, pine needles, leaves — over the ribs until it is at least 3 feet (0.9 m) thick: the thicker the better.
steps.5: Put a layer of insulating material 2 feet (0.6 m) thick inside the shelter.
steps.6: At the entrance, pile insulating material that you can pull into the entrance from inside to close it — or build a door.
steps.7: Finally, lay branches or other material on top of the debris, so that a storm does not blow it away.

shelter-debris-hut.works: For warmth and ease of building, the debris hut is one of the best shelters: when shelter is essential to survival, build this one.
shelter-debris-hut.reliability: At least 6 to 12 inches (15⁠–⁠30 cm) of insulation above you is needed to keep the heat in. Natural shelters usually take the most time and energy to build: gather all the materials first, and choose a site that saves effort.
shelter-debris-hut.mistakes: Too thin a layer of debris: the thicker, the better. Starting to build before all the materials — frame, covering, bedding and cord — have been gathered.

shelter-bedding.title: Bedding and warmth in a shelter

steps.1: Put a layer of insulation between you and the cold ground: a sleeping pad, seat cushions or extra clothing; if these are scarce, ferns and grass; in a conifer forest, boughs.
steps.2: Make natural bedding at least 12 inches (30 cm) thick, so that it still insulates when pressed down. Fluff it up between uses and add material.
steps.3: Pine boughs, moss and grasses can also insulate the shelter itself.
steps.4: Seal all the openings of the shelter except the ventilation holes. Keep the vents open, especially if you use candles, fuel gel or small oil lamps: they produce carbon monoxide.
steps.5: A fire outside the shelter: put the opening of the shelter at 90 degrees to the prevailing wind, so sparks and smoke are not blown in if the wind turns, as often happens in the mountains in the morning and evening. The best distance from fire to shelter is about 3 feet (0.9 m).

shelter-bedding.works: At rest, you can lose as much as 80 percent of your body heat to the ground; a layer of insulation between you and the ground reduces this loss.
shelter-bedding.reliability: Insulation only “somewhat” controls the loss of heat to the ground, and bedding that has been pressed down insulates less: fluff it up and add to it.
shelter-bedding.mistakes: Lying straight on the ground. Closing every opening while a candle or lamp burns: carbon monoxide. Making the fire too close to the shelter, or in front of an opening that faces the wind.

direction-shadow.title: Directions from a shadow

steps.1: Put a stick or branch into the ground at a level spot where it casts a clear shadow. Mark the tip of the shadow with a stone, a twig or the like: this first mark is always west (see the picture).
steps.2: Wait 10 to 15 minutes, until the tip of the shadow has moved a few inches. Mark its new position in the same way.
steps.3: Draw a straight line through the two marks: this is roughly the east–west line.
steps.4: Stand with the first mark (west) on your left: north is in front of you, east is on your right and south is behind you.
steps.5: You need not look for a large level spot: the stick may lean, and a flat spot the size of your hand is enough. Any fixed object — the end of a branch, say — serves as well as a stick, because only the tip of the shadow is marked.

6.text: A more accurate way, around noon (see the second picture):

items.1: put a stick upright where its shadow is at least 12 inches (30 cm) long, and mark the tip of the shadow 5 to 10 minutes before noon;
items.2: draw an arc around the stick with the shadow as its radius — with a string, a shoelace or a second stick;
items.3: after noon the shadow grows longer again: mark the spot where its tip touches the arc a second time;
items.4: a straight line through the two marks is the east–west line.

direction-shadow.works: The sun rises in the east and sets in the west, and shadows move the opposite way. In the Northern Hemisphere, shadows move from west to east and point north at noon.
direction-shadow.reliability: The sun rarely rises due east or sets due west, and there is some seasonal variation: the line you get is approximate. The manual says the first way does not work far north and far south, beyond about 66° latitude, because of the position of the sun above the horizon; the noon way is more accurate and works at all latitudes below 66°, all year round.
direction-shadow.mistakes: Mixing up the marks: the first mark is always west, the second east. Starting the noon way too late: the first mark must be made before noon.

direction-watch.title: Directions from a watch

steps.1: You need an ordinary watch with hands.
steps.2: In the northern temperate zone, hold the watch so that the hour hand points at the sun (see the picture).
steps.3: South lies midway between the hour hand and the 12, if the watch shows standard time. If it shows summer time (daylight saving time), the north–south line lies midway between the hour hand and the 1.
steps.4: If you are not sure which end of the line is north: before noon the sun is in the east, and after noon in the west.
steps.5: If you only have a digital watch, draw a clock face showing the right time on a circle of paper, or on the ground, and use it in the same way.

direction-watch.works: With an ordinary watch with hands you can find the approximate true north and south when the sun is out.
direction-watch.reliability: The watch method can be inaccurate, especially in the lower latitudes, and may make you walk in circles. The rule above is for the northern temperate zone only; in the southern temperate zone it is different.
direction-watch.mistakes: Forgetting summer time: then the line runs between the hour hand and the 1, not the 12. Pointing the 12 at the sun instead of the hour hand: that is the way of the southern temperate zone.

direction-stars.title: North by the North Star

steps.1: On a clear night, find the Big Dipper (Ursa Major): seven stars in the shape of a dipper (see the picture).
steps.2: The two stars at the outer edge of its bowl are the “pointer stars”. In your mind, draw a line from the lower one to the upper one and extend it about five times the distance between them: the North Star (Polaris) lies on this line.
steps.3: You can also use Cassiopeia: five stars in the shape of a “W”, one side of which looks flatter. Halve the angle on its flatter side and extend that line about five times the distance between the bottom and the top of the “W”. The North Star lies between Cassiopeia and the Big Dipper.
steps.4: The Big Dipper and Cassiopeia are generally opposite each other and turn around the North Star: using both together helps prevent confusion.
steps.5: True north lies straight below the North Star: draw an imaginary line from it down to the earth.
steps.6: The moon gives only a rough east–west direction: if it rises before the sun has set, its lit side faces west; if it rises after midnight, its lit side faces east.

direction-stars.works: The North Star practically stays in one place: it moves only 1.08 degrees around the northern celestial pole. This way is for the northern sky.
direction-stars.reliability: The North Star is the last star of the handle of the Little Dipper, whose seven stars are rather dim and hard to see near towns and cities; it can be confused with the Big Dipper.
direction-stars.mistakes: Taking a star of the Big Dipper for the North Star. Relying on the moon for more than a rough direction.

direction-compass.title: An improvised compass

steps.1: You need a piece of iron or steel — a needle or a flat double-edged razor blade — and a thread or a long hair to hang it from.
steps.2: Magnetize it: stroke it slowly, always in one direction only, on a piece of silk or through your hair — or stroke one end of it again and again with a magnet.
steps.3: Hang the needle or blade from the hair or thread: it slowly turns to lie along the north–south line.
steps.4: Or float it: pass the magnetized needle through your hair to oil it and lay it gently on still water — or lay it on a small piece of cork, a leaf or tape floating on the water. It slowly turns north–south.
steps.5: With a battery of at least 2 volts and an insulated wire, you can magnetize the metal electrically: form a coil from the wire, touch its ends to the battery’s terminals, and move one end of the metal in and out of the coil again and again. If the wire is bare, first wrap the metal in a thin strip of paper or a leaf.

direction-compass.works: A magnetized needle, hung from a hair or floating on water, gradually lines up north–south.
direction-compass.reliability: The manual says only that the needle lines up along the north–south line; it does not say how to tell its north end. Where north is, the shadow and the watch show (other cards in this section).
direction-compass.mistakes: Stroking back and forth: always stroke in one direction only. Hanging the needle from a metal thread: use a string that is not metal.

direction-signs.title: Moss, stumps and slopes: signs to treat with care

steps.1: Moss on a tree cannot be relied on to show north: on some trees it grows all around. Where it grows, it is actually lusher on the south-facing side in the Northern Hemisphere.
steps.2: Stumps: if several felled trees are around, compare their stumps. Growth is more vigorous on the side towards the equator, where the growth rings are more widely spaced; on the side towards the pole they are closer together.
steps.3: Slopes: in the Northern Hemisphere, north-facing slopes get less sun than south-facing ones, so they are cooler and damper. In summer, north-facing slopes keep patches of snow; in winter, south-facing slopes and the south sides of boulders and large rocks lose their snow first.
steps.4: Wind helps only where it blows from a prevailing direction and you know what that direction is.

direction-signs.works: Differences in plants and moisture between north- and south-facing slopes can help you find direction.
direction-signs.reliability: These are signs, not instruments: moss is not reliable at all, and stumps tell you something only when there are several of them to compare.
direction-signs.mistakes: Using the moss on a tree as a compass. Judging by a single stump. Trusting the wind without knowing its prevailing direction.

cordage-fibres.title: Cordage from fibres

steps.1: Use what you have: unravel a cotton web belt into string, or twist or braid several strands of parachute cord, or strips of a sheet, into a rope (see the picture). Parachute cord can also be taken apart into its outer cover and its inner strands.
steps.2: Test natural material before you make cordage from it: pull on a length of it; twist it between your fingers and roll the fibres together; if it holds and does not snap, tie an overhand knot in it and tighten it gently. If the knot does not break, the material will work.
steps.3: Fibres from the inner bark of some trees — such as linden, elm, white oak, mulberry, chestnut, red and white cedar — make cord. Test it to be sure it is strong enough; braiding several strands together makes it stronger.
steps.4: Twisting: gather long, strong, tested fibres into loose strands of even thickness — about 15 to 30 fibres to a strand — and twist each strand clockwise. Then twist two, three or four strands together counterclockwise, while you keep twisting the strands that are not yet laid up clockwise (see the second picture). Each strand must be of equal twist and thickness.
steps.5: Alone, you can spin cord by rolling the fibres between the flat of your hand and your thigh, feeding in new fibre with the other hand.

6.text: A three-strand braid, if no one can help you spin:

items.1: pass the right-hand strand over the strand to its left;
items.2: pass the left-hand strand over the strand to its right;
items.3: repeat, alternately from left and right.

cordage-fibres.works: Almost any natural fibrous material can be spun into good serviceable rope or cord, and many materials 12 to 24 inches (30⁠–⁠61 cm) long or more can be braided.
cordage-fibres.reliability: The strength of home-made rope varies widely: for safety, always count on the lowest figure. Natural rope is destroyed if its fibres are cut with a sharp rock or knife, and it loses strength if it is not kept clean. Spinning cord by hand is slow if a long length is needed.
cordage-fibres.mistakes: Strands of uneven twist, thickness or tension: each strand must be of equal twist and thickness. Letting one strand twist around the other while laying up. Using material you have not tested.

knot-square.title: Square knot

steps.1: Words: the running end is the free, working end of a rope; the standing part is the rest of it; a bight is a U-shaped bend in the rope.
steps.2: Use the square knot to tie together two ropes of equal thickness.
steps.3: Lay the running ends of the two ropes together, pointing in opposite directions, and pass the running end of one rope under the standing part of the other.
steps.4: Bring the two running ends up, away from where they cross, and cross them again.
steps.5: When each running end lies parallel to its own standing part, pull the two ends tight (see the picture).
steps.6: To untie it, take hold of the bends of the two bights and pull the knot apart.

knot-square.works: A true square knot draws tighter under strain, and it can be untied easily.
knot-square.reliability: If a running end does not lie parallel to its own standing part, the knot is a “granny knot”: it slips under strain, so do not use it. If the ends lie parallel but not opposite each other, it is a “thief knot”: it slips under strain and is hard to untie.
knot-square.mistakes: Tying a granny or a thief knot instead of a square knot. Leaving the knot loose: a loosely tied knot can easily deform under strain and slip or come undone.

knot-sheet-bend.title: Sheet bend: joining ropes of different thickness

steps.1: Use the single sheet bend to tie together two dry ropes of different thickness (the words: see the card “Square knot”).
steps.2: Make a bight in the thicker rope.
steps.3: Pass the running end of the thinner rope through the bight, around both parts of the thicker rope and back under the thinner rope itself; then pull it tight (see the picture).
steps.4: Double sheet bend: before you pull it tight, take one extra turn with the thinner rope around both sides of the bight, then tighten (see the second picture).

knot-sheet-bend.works: The single sheet bend draws tight under light loads. The double sheet bend is better for joining ropes of equal or different thickness, for wet ropes and for tying a rope to an eye: it does not slip or draw tight under heavy loads.
knot-sheet-bend.reliability: The single sheet bend is only for dry ropes, and it may loosen or slip when the tension is released.
knot-sheet-bend.mistakes: Using the single sheet bend on wet ropes, or trusting it after the load comes off: use the double sheet bend.

knot-bowline.title: Bowline: a loop at the end of a rope

steps.1: Pass the running end through the object you are tying to, and form a small loop in the standing part (the words: see the card “Square knot”).
steps.2: Pass the running end up through the loop from underneath, around the standing part, and back down through the loop from the top: it goes down beside the rope that comes up through the loop.
steps.3: Pull the knot tight (see the picture).
steps.4: For a loop away from the end of the rope, tie a bowline on a bight: double the rope, form a loop as for the bowline, pass the end of the doubled part up through the loop, back down around the whole knot, and tighten. It is easily untied and does not slip.

knot-bowline.works: The bowline is a useful knot for forming a loop at the end of a rope, and it is easy to untie.
knot-bowline.reliability: Dress and set every knot — straighten its parts and tighten them so they bind on one another: neglecting this can reduce the knot’s strength by 50 percent.
knot-bowline.mistakes: Leaving the knot loose or badly dressed. Passing the running end the wrong way through the loop: it goes up from underneath, around the standing part and back down from the top.

knot-clove-hitch.title: Clove hitch: a rope to a pole

steps.1: Use it to fasten a rope to a pole, post or pipe; it can be tied at any point of the rope. Lashings begin and end with it.
steps.2: In the middle of a rope: make two turns close together and twist them so that the two loops lie back to back; slip both loops over the pole (see the picture, “At center of rope”).
steps.3: At the end of a rope: pass the rope around the pole in two turns, so that the first turn crosses the standing part and the running end comes up under itself on the second turn (“At end of rope”).
steps.4: Tying a line to a tent stake: the line passes in front of the stake first and then under itself.

knot-clove-hitch.works: A hitch secures a rope around a pole or post so that it holds for the time being but can readily be undone.
knot-clove-hitch.reliability: A hitch is meant to hold temporarily: it can readily be undone.
knot-clove-hitch.mistakes: Twisting the two loops so that they do not lie back to back. Leaving it loose.

knot-half-hitches.title: Round turn and two half hitches

steps.1: Use it to tie a rope to a pole or tree where you need a good anchor and a high load would make other knots jam and be hard to untie.
steps.2: Round turn: take the rope around the pole so that the running end leaves the circle in the same general direction as the standing part.
steps.3: Half hitch: pass the running end around the standing part and back under itself.
steps.4: Make a second half hitch in the same way, and pull tight (see the pictures).
steps.5: Two half hitches alone are a quick way to tie a rope to a pole: pass the running end around the pole, then make the two half hitches around the standing part.

knot-half-hitches.works: It is the main anchor knot when a good anchor is needed and high loads would make other knots jam; it is most used to anchor a rope to a pole or tree.
knot-half-hitches.reliability: A single half hitch is not a very secure knot: it is only for temporarily securing the free end of a rope, and it tends to undo itself without a load.
knot-half-hitches.mistakes: Trusting a single half hitch. Leaving the half hitches loose.

lashing-square.title: Lashing poles together

steps.1: Square lashing fastens one pole at right angles to another (see the picture).
steps.2: Start with a clove hitch around the upright pole, just under where the crosspiece will lie.
steps.3: Lay three or four turns: around the crosspiece the rope goes outside the previous turn, around the upright pole inside it. Keep the rope tight.
steps.4: Make two or three frapping turns between the poles, around the turns, and pull them tight: this binds the poles firmly together.
steps.5: Finish with a clove hitch: the text of the manual says around the same pole you started on; its picture shows it on the crosspiece.
steps.6: Diagonal lashing, where poles cross: start with a clove hitch around both poles where they cross; take three turns around both, lying side by side, then three more crosswise over them; pull tight, add a couple of frapping turns between the poles, and finish with a clove hitch on the pole you started on.
steps.7: Shear lashing, for poles side by side: lay them loosely beside each other, start with a clove hitch on an outer pole, make seven or eight turns around all of them with frapping turns between each pole, and finish with a clove hitch on the pole at the other side.

lashing-square.works: Lashings bind poles for shelters and racks: the square lashing holds one pole at right angles to another; the shear lashing joins poles side by side.
lashing-square.reliability: The turns hold the poles together, and the frapping turns make them tight. The manual’s picture and text differ on where to finish the square lashing (step 5).
lashing-square.mistakes: Laying the turns of a diagonal lashing on top of each other: they lie beside each other. Leaving out the frapping turns. Letting the rope go slack.

shelter-clothing.title: Clothing: your first shelter

steps.1: Your clothing is your first shelter: keep it in as good a condition as you can, and wear it properly.
steps.2: Clean: keep your clothing clean. Clothes matted with dirt and grease lose much of their insulation: heat escapes more easily through crushed or filled-up air pockets.
steps.3: Do not overheat: when you get too hot, you sweat and your clothing takes up the moisture — damp clothing insulates less, and as the sweat evaporates, your body cools. Before you start to sweat, open your jacket a little, take off an inner layer or your heavy mittens, or throw back your hood.
steps.4: Loose and in layers: tight clothing and footwear restrict blood circulation and invite cold injuries. Several layers of light clothing are better than one equally thick layer, because there is still air between the layers; and you can take layers off or add them.
steps.5: Dry: wet clothing can take heat away from the body up to 25 times faster than dry clothing. If you have water-repellent clothing, wear it as the outer layer.
steps.6: Drying: put wet clothes on your rucksack, in the sun and wind, or keep damp clothes close to your body; where you stay, make a drying rack or a line. Near a fire, use the three-second rule: hold the back of your hand where the clothes will be — if you can comfortably keep it there for three seconds or more, it is not too close. Watch the clothes so that they do not fall into the fire. Dry leather slowly.
steps.7: Look your clothing over now and then for worn spots and tears, and mend it before the holes become too large to patch or sew; patches can be made from cloth or tape.
steps.8: Socks: keep your feet dry — carry spare socks and change them as needed. Wool keeps its insulation when wet; cotton, once wet, loses about 90 percent of its insulation and is very difficult to dry.

shelter-clothing.works: Your clothing is the shelter you always have with you: it has to keep you dry, warm or cool, out of the sun and away from insects.
shelter-clothing.reliability: Clothing protects you only when it is in good condition and worn properly. Polypropylene, a common synthetic base layer, has a low melting point: take care when you dry it near a fire.
shelter-clothing.mistakes: Sweating in the cold. Tight clothes or boots. Drying clothes too close to the fire, or without watching them. Leaving tears until they are too large to mend.

chest-penetrating.title: Penetrating chest injury

steps.1: Before giving help, make sure there is no danger; only when there is none, go on to the next step.
steps.2: Calm the person and explain what you are going to do.
steps.3: Call emergency medical help and follow the instructions of the dispatcher.
steps.4: Help the person into the position most comfortable for them.

5.text: Put an occlusive (airtight) dressing on the chest wound:

items.1: ask the person to breathe out as far as they can and put an occlusive dressing on the wound. If you have none, put on an improvised occlusive dressing made of a material that does not let air through and fix it on all sides with adhesive tape. If that is not possible either, consider pressing on the wound with your palm in a rubber glove;
items.2: check the person’s condition, and if it suddenly gets much worse, take the dressing off;
items.3: if there are several wounds, put an occlusive dressing on all of them.

steps.6: If there is a foreign object in the chest wound, leave it in place and, if possible, fix it securely. The foreign object may be removed from the chest wound only if it gets in the way of cardiopulmonary resuscitation.
steps.7: Watch over the person constantly until the emergency (ambulance) team arrives.
steps.8: Cover the person with a thermal blanket or a blanket.
steps.9: If the person’s condition gets worse before the emergency (ambulance) team arrives, call emergency medical help again.
steps.10: If you can, gather as much information as possible from the person about how the injury happened. Pass all of it on to the emergency (ambulance) team or to the dispatcher.
steps.11: If the person loses consciousness before the emergency (ambulance) team arrives, go to the procedure for sudden cardiac arrest in an adult or in a child.

chest-penetrating.works: A “penetrating chest injury” is a wound of the chest with signs that it goes into the pleural cavity, whatever caused the injury. Signs of a penetrating chest injury: a wound in the chest from which bright, frothy blood flows; a wound in the chest through which air can be heard moving, including a sucking sound with every breath in; several wounds in the chest lying in the same projection (one behind the other).
chest-penetrating.reliability: The procedure is written for people “who have no medical education but must give first aid as part of their duties”. The order does not assess how reliable the steps are. About the occlusive dressing the order says: “check the person’s condition, and if it suddenly gets much worse, take the dressing off”.
chest-penetrating.mistakes: Taking a foreign object out of the wound. The order: “if there is a foreign object in the chest wound, leave it in place and, if possible, fix it securely”.

chest-blunt.title: Blunt chest injury

steps.1: Before giving help, make sure there is no danger; only when there is none, go on to the next step.
steps.2: Calm the person and explain what you are going to do.
steps.3: Call emergency medical help and follow the instructions of the dispatcher.
steps.4: Help the person into the position most comfortable for them.
steps.5: Watch over the person constantly until the emergency (ambulance) team arrives.
steps.6: Cover the person with a thermal blanket or a blanket.
steps.7: If the person’s condition gets worse before the emergency (ambulance) team arrives, call emergency medical help again.
steps.8: If you can, gather as much information as possible from the person about how the injury happened. Pass all of it on to the emergency (ambulance) team or to the dispatcher of the emergency medical service.
steps.9: If the person loses consciousness before the emergency (ambulance) team arrives, go to the procedure for sudden cardiac arrest in an adult or in a child.

chest-blunt.works: A “blunt chest injury” means signs of a blunt injury to the chest, with signs of broken ribs and/or damage to the organs inside the chest, whatever caused the injury. Signs of a blunt chest injury: bruises or haematomas on the chest; subcutaneous emphysema — a sound like creaking snow when the soft tissues are pressed; broken ribs: pain in the chest, a forced posture; the two sides of the chest are not symmetrical; bleeding into the pleural cavity: fast, shallow breathing, pale, cold, moist skin, general weakness, confusion; torn lung tissue: pain in the chest, fast, shallow breathing, a feeling of not getting enough air, pale, cold, moist skin, general weakness, confusion.
chest-blunt.reliability: The procedure is written for people “who have no medical education but must give first aid as part of their duties”. The order does not assess how reliable the steps are.
chest-blunt.mistakes: The order does not name them separately.

abdomen-penetrating.title: Penetrating abdominal injury

steps.1: Before giving help, make sure there is no danger; only when there is none, go on to the next step.
steps.2: Calm the person and explain what you are going to do.
steps.3: Call emergency medical help and follow the instructions of the dispatcher.
steps.4: Help the person into the position most comfortable for them.

5.text: Put a dressing on the wound:

items.1: put a clean, sterile gauze dressing over the whole wound and fix it carefully with adhesive tape;
items.2: if organs from inside the abdomen are in the wound, do not push them back into the abdomen before putting on the gauze dressing;
items.3: if an object is stuck in the wound, do not take it out; fix it securely in the wound. If the object falls out of the wound by itself while you are giving first aid, carefully put it aside and hand it over to the emergency (ambulance) team.

steps.6: Watch over the person constantly until the emergency (ambulance) team arrives.
steps.7: Cover the person with a thermal blanket or a blanket.
steps.8: If the person’s condition gets worse before the emergency (ambulance) team arrives, call emergency medical help again.
steps.9: If you can, gather as much information as possible from the person about how the injury happened. Pass all of it on to the emergency (ambulance) team or to the dispatcher of the emergency medical service.
steps.10: If the person loses consciousness before the emergency (ambulance) team arrives, go to the procedure for sudden cardiac arrest in an adult or in a child.

abdomen-penetrating.works: A “penetrating abdominal injury” is a wound within the set anatomical landmarks with signs that it goes into the abdominal cavity, whatever caused the injury. Signs of a penetrating abdominal injury: organs from inside the abdomen in the wound; several wounds in the abdomen lying in the same projection (one behind the other); an object stuck in the wound; a wound and signs of damage to the organs inside the abdomen with bleeding: fast, shallow breathing; pale, moist, cold skin; impaired consciousness.
abdomen-penetrating.reliability: The procedure is written for people “who have no medical education but must give first aid as part of their duties”. The order does not assess how reliable the steps are.
abdomen-penetrating.mistakes: “If organs from inside the abdomen are in the wound, do not push them back into the abdomen before putting on the gauze dressing”; “if an object is stuck in the wound, do not take it out”.

abdomen-blunt.title: Blunt abdominal injury

steps.1: Before giving help, make sure there is no danger; only when there is none, go on to the next step.
steps.2: Calm the person and explain what you are going to do.
steps.3: Call emergency medical help and follow the instructions of the dispatcher.
steps.4: Help the person into the position most comfortable for them. If there are signs of shock, put the person in the shock position.
steps.5: Cover the person with a thermal blanket or a blanket.
steps.6: Watch over the person constantly until the emergency (ambulance) team arrives.
steps.7: If the person’s condition gets worse before the emergency (ambulance) team arrives, call emergency medical help again.
steps.8: If you can, gather as much information as possible from the person about how the injury happened. Pass all of it on to the emergency (ambulance) team or to the dispatcher.
steps.9: If the person loses consciousness before the emergency (ambulance) team arrives, go to the procedure for sudden cardiac arrest in an adult or in a child.

abdomen-blunt.works: A “blunt abdominal injury” means signs of a blunt injury to the organs in the abdomen, including signs of internal bleeding, whatever caused the injury. Signs of a blunt abdominal injury: bruises and a haematoma on the front and/or side wall of the abdomen; signs of internal bleeding: fast, shallow breathing; pale, moist, cold skin; impaired consciousness; pain in the abdomen.
abdomen-blunt.reliability: The procedure is written for people “who have no medical education but must give first aid as part of their duties”. The order does not assess how reliable the steps are.
abdomen-blunt.mistakes: The order does not name them separately.

amputation.title: Traumatic amputation

steps.1: Before giving help, make sure there is no danger; only when there is none, go on to the next step.
steps.2: If there is massive external bleeding, act according to the procedure for massive external bleeding.
steps.3: If there is a traumatic amputation above the wrist or above the foot and there is no bleeding, a tourniquet must be applied all the same.
steps.4: Calm the person and explain what you are going to do.
steps.5: Call emergency medical help and follow the instructions of the dispatcher.
steps.6: Put a clean, sterile dressing on the stump.
steps.7: Put the person in the shock position.
steps.8: Keep the stump still (immobilise it).
steps.9: Cover the person with a thermal blanket or a blanket.
steps.10: Watch over the person constantly until the emergency (ambulance) team arrives.
steps.11: Find the amputated part of the body.
steps.12: Wrap the amputated part of the body in sterile gauze or a clean cloth.
steps.13: Put the amputated part in a plastic bag (if possible, press the air out of it).
steps.14: Put the bag in a container filled with cold water or ice.
steps.15: If the person’s condition gets worse before the emergency (ambulance) team arrives, call the emergency medical dispatcher again.
steps.16: If you can, gather as much information as possible from the person about how the injury happened. Pass all of it on to the emergency (ambulance) team or to the dispatcher.
steps.17: If the person loses consciousness before the emergency (ambulance) team arrives, go to the procedure for sudden cardiac arrest in an adult or in a child.

amputation.works: A “traumatic amputation” is an emergency in which part or all of a limb (or another part of the body) is cut off or torn off by a mechanical force.
amputation.reliability: The procedure is written for people “who have no medical education but must give first aid as part of their duties”. The order does not assess how reliable the steps are.
amputation.mistakes: The order does not name them separately.

crush.title: Crush syndrome (long compression)

steps.1: Before giving help, make sure there is no danger; only when there is none, go on to the next step.
steps.2: Calm the person and explain what you are going to do.
steps.3: If possible, find out exactly when the compression began. If the person is unconscious, assume that more than 10 minutes have passed.
steps.4: Call the emergency medical dispatcher at once, give them the information they need clearly, follow their instructions if necessary and answer all their questions.

5.text: If less than 10 minutes have passed since the compression began, free the crushed part of the body:

items.1: if there is a wound and massive external bleeding, act according to the procedure for massive external bleeding;
items.2: if there are signs of a fracture, act according to the procedure for a suspected broken limb;
items.3: if there are signs of shock, act according to the procedure for suspected shock.

steps.6: If more than 10 minutes have passed since the compression began, do not free the crushed part of the person’s body.
steps.7: If the person has to be moved out urgently but more than 10 minutes have passed since the compression began, apply a tourniquet to the limb before freeing the crushed part.
steps.8: Cover the person with a thermal blanket or a blanket.
steps.9: Watch over the person constantly until the emergency (ambulance) team arrives.
steps.10: If the person’s condition gets worse before the emergency (ambulance) team arrives, call the emergency medical dispatcher again.
steps.11: If you can, gather as much information as possible from the person about how the injury happened. Pass all of it on to the emergency (ambulance) team or to the dispatcher.
steps.12: If the person loses consciousness before the emergency (ambulance) team arrives, go to the procedure for sudden cardiac arrest in an adult or in a child.

crush.works: “Crush syndrome” (long compression) is an emergency in which outside pressure acts on a part of the person’s body, so that its blood supply is disturbed, and as a result the soft tissues suffer from a lack of blood (ischaemia) and are damaged.
crush.reliability: The procedure is written for people “who have no medical education but must give first aid as part of their duties”. The order does not assess how reliable the steps are.
crush.mistakes: “If more than 10 minutes have passed since the compression began, do not free the crushed part of the person’s body”.

poisoning.title: Suspected poisoning by an unknown substance

steps.1: Before giving help, make sure there is no danger to yourself, the people around or the person; only when there is none, go on to the next step.
steps.2: Calm the person and explain what you are going to do.

3.text: When looking over the scene, watch for signs that may point to acute poisoning:

items.1: an unpleasant, sharp smell;
items.2: open or overturned containers, containers of medicines and of alcoholic drinks;
items.3: an open medicine kit, used syringes and the like.

steps.4: Find out what exactly the person took and how much.
steps.5: Call emergency medical help and follow the instructions of the dispatcher.
steps.6: If the person is unconscious but breathing normally, put them in the stable (recovery) position.
steps.7: If the poison has got into the eyes and/or onto the skin, rinse the affected area with plenty of clean water at room temperature for at least 15–20 minutes. If there are chemical burns, put a sterile dressing on the burn (after rinsing with water).
steps.8: Keep any containers, syringes, packaging and the like that you find, and hand them over to the emergency (ambulance) team.
steps.9: Watch over the person constantly until the emergency (ambulance) team arrives.
steps.10: If the person’s condition gets worse before the emergency (ambulance) team arrives, call emergency medical help again.
steps.11: If you can, gather as much information as possible from the person or the people around about how the poisoning happened. Pass all of it on to the emergency (ambulance) team or to the dispatcher.
steps.12: If the person loses consciousness before the emergency (ambulance) team arrives, go to the procedure for sudden cardiac arrest in an adult or in a child.
steps.13: While doing cardiopulmonary resuscitation, keep the toxic substances from acting on the person giving first aid.

poisoning.works: “Acute poisoning by an unknown substance” is an emergency caused by poisonous substances, whatever way they entered the body, with a marked worsening of the person’s condition. Toxic substances can enter the body: through the digestive tract — with food or when poisonous substances touch the lining of the mouth (medicines, caustic substances, detergents, pesticides, mushrooms, plants and many other chemicals); through the airways — by breathing in poisonous gases, vapours and aerosols (carbon monoxide; nitrogen oxide; vapours of chlorine, ammonia, glue, dyes, organic solvents and the like); through the skin and mucous membranes — when poisonous liquids or aerosols get onto the skin or into the eyes (solvents, pesticides and the like); by injection — bites of insects, animals or snakes, and when medicines or drugs are injected. Signs that point to acute poisoning: a feeling of “sand” or a stinging pain in the eyes, discomfort from light; burns on the lips, tongue or skin; pain in the mouth, throat, chest or abdomen that gets worse when swallowing and breathing; more saliva than usual, nausea, vomiting (with a particular smell, remains of the poison, blood), diarrhoea; breathing problems (choking, noisy breathing, a changed voice, cough); sweating, unusual behaviour (agitation, delirium); muscle twitching, seizures, loss of consciousness; an unusual skin colour (pale, crimson, bluish).
poisoning.reliability: The procedure is written for people “who have no medical education but must give first aid as part of their duties”. The order does not assess how reliable the steps are.
poisoning.mistakes: The order does not name them separately.

seizures.title: Seizures

steps.1: Before giving help, make sure there is no danger to yourself, the people around or the person; only when there is none, go on to the next step.
steps.2: Call the emergency medical dispatcher at once, give them the information they need clearly, follow their instructions if necessary and answer all their questions.

items.1: move the person onto a flat surface;
items.2: put a soft blanket under the person’s head;
items.3: hold the person’s head for the whole time of the seizure;
items.4: do not use too much force to hold the person during the seizure;
items.5: do not force the person’s mouth open, including with any improvised tools;
items.6: do not force any liquid into the person or give them any medicines.

items.1: if the person is unconscious, put them in the stable (recovery) position;
items.2: if the person is conscious, calm them and explain what you are going to do next.

steps.5: Watch over the person constantly until the emergency (ambulance) team arrives.
steps.6: If the person’s condition gets worse before the emergency (ambulance) team arrives, call the emergency medical dispatcher again.
steps.7: If you can, gather as much information as possible from the person or the people around about how the seizures began. Pass all of it on to the emergency (ambulance) team or to the dispatcher of the emergency medical service.
steps.8: If the person loses consciousness before the emergency (ambulance) team arrives, go to the procedure for sudden cardiac arrest in an adult or in a child.

seizures.works: “Seizures” are an emergency caused by disturbed brain activity, with involuntary, uncontrolled contractions of the body’s muscles. Seizures can be caused by: a head (brain) injury; disorders of the central nervous system of various origins; poisoning; hypoglycaemia; fever.
seizures.reliability: The procedure is written for people “who have no medical education but must give first aid as part of their duties”. The order does not assess how reliable the steps are.
seizures.mistakes: “Do not use too much force to hold the person during the seizure”; “do not force the person’s mouth open, including with any improvised tools”; “do not force any liquid into the person or give them any medicines”.

eye-injury.title: Eye injuries

steps.1: Before giving help, make sure there is no danger to yourself, the people around or the person; only when there is none, go on to the next step.
steps.2: Calm the person and explain what you are going to do next.
steps.3: Call emergency medical help and follow the instructions of the dispatcher.

items.1: put a protective eye shield over the injured eye, or, if there is none, something else that keeps pressure off the eyeball;
items.2: put another clean gauze pad over the shield and fix it carefully, without pressing too hard on the injured eye;
items.3: if there is a foreign object in the wound, do not take it out; fix it securely in the wound;
items.4: do not try to put the eye back if it has come out of its socket.

5.text: If chemicals have got into the eye:

items.1: rinse the affected eye with plenty of clean running water for 10–20 minutes;
items.2: take care not to contaminate the healthy eye while rinsing;
items.3: wear gloves while rinsing if you can, and take them off carefully when you have finished.

steps.6: Watch over the person constantly until the emergency (ambulance) team arrives.
steps.7: If the person’s condition gets worse before the emergency (ambulance) team arrives, call emergency medical help again.
steps.8: If you can, gather as much information as possible from the person or the people around about how the eyes were injured. Pass all of it on to the emergency (ambulance) team or to the dispatcher.
steps.9: If the person loses consciousness before the emergency (ambulance) team arrives, go to the procedure for sudden cardiac arrest in an adult or in a child.

eye-injury.works: An “eye injury” is an emergency caused by an injury or by chemicals getting into the eyes, which can lead to a partial or complete loss of sight.
eye-injury.reliability: The procedure is written for people “who have no medical education but must give first aid as part of their duties”. The order does not assess how reliable the steps are.
eye-injury.mistakes: “If there is a foreign object in the wound, do not take it out”; “do not try to put the eye back if it has come out of its socket”; “take care not to contaminate the healthy eye while rinsing”.

hypoglycemia.title: Hypoglycaemia (low blood sugar)

steps.1: Before giving help, make sure there is no danger to yourself, the people around or the person; only when there is none, go on to the next step.
steps.2: Calm the person and explain what you are going to do next.
steps.3: Call emergency medical help and follow the instructions of the dispatcher.

4.text: If the person is conscious and able to swallow:

items.1: give a glucose or dextrose tablet (15–20 grams);
items.2: if there are no glucose tablets, give food you have that contains as much glucose: sweets; a sugar cube; half a glass of sweet warm tea or juice and the like;
items.3: if the signs of hypoglycaemia have not gone after 15 minutes, give glucose or food containing glucose again;
items.4: if the person feels better after taking glucose, encourage them to eat;
items.5: if a child has hypoglycaemia and refuses to take glucose or food, consider putting half a teaspoon of sugar under their tongue.

steps.5: If possible, and if the rescuer has had the training for it, measure the blood glucose level before and after the person takes glucose.
steps.6: If the person’s condition gets worse before the emergency (ambulance) team arrives, call emergency medical help again.
steps.7: If you can, gather as much information as possible from the person or the people around about what may have caused the hypoglycaemia. Pass all of it on to the emergency (ambulance) team or to the dispatcher.
steps.8: If the person loses consciousness before the emergency (ambulance) team arrives, go to the procedure for sudden cardiac arrest in an adult or in a child.

hypoglycemia.works: “Hypoglycaemia” is an emergency caused by a fall in the level of glucose in the blood, which brings about typical changes in the person. Signs of hypoglycaemia: sudden impaired consciousness: dizziness, fainting; unusual behaviour (mood swings, aggression, confusion, loss of concentration, signs that look like being drunk).
hypoglycemia.reliability: The procedure is written for people “who have no medical education but must give first aid as part of their duties”. The order does not assess how reliable the steps are. Measure the blood glucose level only “if possible, and if the rescuer has had the training for it”.
hypoglycemia.mistakes: The order does not name them separately. Glucose or food is given only “if the person is conscious and able to swallow”.

trauma.title: Injured person: primary and secondary survey

steps.1: Before giving help, make sure there is no danger to yourself, the people around or the person; only when there is none, go on to the next step.

items.1: as you approach the person, assess their age, sex, weight and position, including in relation to the objects around them;
items.2: assess how active the person is: oriented in time and place, making purposeful movements, agitated and so on;
items.3: look for signs of massive external bleeding;
items.4: speak to the person: “Can you hear me? My name is (say your name). Can I help you?”;
items.5: approach the person from the side where they can see you, so as to limit the movements of their head.

3.text: Go on to the primary survey:

items.1: if the person is conscious and has signs of massive external bleeding, stop the bleeding according to the procedure for massive external bleeding;
items.2: if the person is unconscious, open the airway by pushing the lower jaw forward (jaw thrust) and check whether they are breathing. While opening the airway, limit the movements of the neck (cervical spine);
items.3: if there is no breathing, go to the procedure for sudden cardiac arrest in an adult;
items.4: if the person is unconscious and breathing, keep the airway open all the time with the methods taught on the relevant courses (jaw thrust, inserting airways);
items.5: once the person’s airway is open, check for penetrating chest wounds; if there are any, go to the procedure for a penetrating chest injury;
items.6: check whether the person has wounds with external bleeding; if there are any, go to the procedure for massive external bleeding;
items.7: if the person has signs of shock, go to the procedure for suspected shock.

4.text: Go on to the secondary survey — examine the person fully for injuries from head to toe:

items.1: if there is a head injury, go to the procedure for a suspected head injury;
items.2: if the eyes are injured, go to the procedure for eye injuries;
items.3: if there is a penetrating chest injury, go to the procedure for a penetrating chest injury;
items.4: if there is a blunt chest injury, go to the procedure for a blunt chest injury;
items.5: if a spinal injury is suspected, go to the procedure for a suspected spinal injury;
items.6: if there is a penetrating abdominal injury, go to the procedure for a penetrating abdominal injury;
items.7: if there is a blunt abdominal injury, go to the procedure for a blunt abdominal injury;
items.8: if there are signs of frostbite, go to the procedure for hypothermia and/or frostbite;
items.9: if there are burns from heat, go to the procedure for burns from heat;
items.10: if there are signs of long compression, go to the procedure for crush syndrome;
items.11: if there is a traumatic amputation, go to the procedure for traumatic amputation;
items.12: if limbs are broken, go to the procedure for a suspected broken limb.

steps.5: Watch over the person constantly until the emergency (ambulance) team arrives.
steps.6: If the person’s condition gets worse before the emergency (ambulance) team arrives, call emergency medical help again.
steps.7: If you can, gather as much information as possible from the person or the people around about how the injury happened. Pass all of it on to the emergency (ambulance) team or to the dispatcher of the emergency medical service.

trauma.works: The “general impression of the injured person” is the information you get while approaching the person, from which you form a first idea of how and in what circumstances the injury happened and of the person’s condition. The “primary survey” is a quick check of the person’s vital functions and, if needed, dealing with conditions that threaten life. The “secondary survey” is finding and assessing the injuries the person has; it is done only when there are no conditions that threaten their life.
trauma.reliability: The procedure is written for people “who have no medical education but must give first aid as part of their duties”. The order does not assess how reliable the steps are. Keep the airway open only “with the methods taught on the relevant courses (jaw thrust, inserting airways)”.
trauma.mistakes: The order does not name them separately.

atp-sub-surface-water.title: Figure 3-11. Sub-surface water

atp-water-filters.title: Figure 3-12. Water filtering systems
atp-water-filters.alt: Two filters. Left: three cloths hung one above the other on a tripod of poles hold grass, sand and charcoal; water drips through them into a box. Right: a plastic bag hung from a branch is filled with layers of rocks, sand and charcoal; water drips out of its bottom.

atp-fire-walls.title: Figure 5-2. Types of firewalls
atp-fire-walls.alt: Two kinds of fire walls made of logs stacked between stakes. Top: a straight wall in front of a lean-to shelter. Bottom: an L-shaped wall with a fire burning in its corner.

atp-fire-lays.title: Figure 5-5. Fire lays
atp-fire-lays.alt: Four ways to lay a fire: tepee — sticks leaning together in a cone; lean-to — sticks leaning against one long stick pushed into the ground at an angle; cross-ditch — two shallow ditches dug in an X, with tinder where they cross; pyramid — two logs on the ground with layers of smaller sticks across them.

atp-convex-lens.title: Figure 5-7. Using a convex lens as a fire-starter
atp-convex-lens.alt: A hand holds a small lens above a heap of tinder; the sun’s rays meet on the tinder, which begins to smoke.

atp-flint-steel.title: Figure 5-8. Flint and steel fire-starter
atp-flint-steel.alt: Two hands: one holds a stone, the other a piece of steel; they strike each other and sparks fly.

atp-bow-drill.title: Figure 5-10. Bow and drill fire-starter
atp-bow-drill.alt: Left: the parts of a bow drill, one above the other — the socket on top, the drill, the bow with its cord wrapped around the drill, and the fire board at the bottom. Right: a kneeling man holds the socket on the drill with one hand and moves the bow with the other; his foot holds the fire board; smoke rises.

atp-natural-shelters.title: Figure 6-1. Types of naturally occurring shelters
atp-natural-shelters.alt: Shelters that are already there: a clump of bushes; a hollow under a large rock; a fallen tree with thick branches; pieces of wood leaning against a fallen trunk; a pit dug in the snow around a tree.

atp-poncho-lean-to.title: Figure 6-2. Poncho lean-to
atp-poncho-lean-to.alt: A poncho tied by its corners between two trees at about waist height and pegged to the ground behind, as a sloping roof; an arrow shows the wind blowing against its back.

atp-debris-hut.title: Figure 6-13. Debris hut
atp-debris-hut.alt: Top: the frame — a long ridgepole resting on a stump, with sticks propped along both sides like ribs. Bottom: the same frame covered with a thick layer of leaves, its entrance by the stump.

atp-shadow-tip.title: Figure 7-8 (part A). Shadow-tip method
atp-shadow-tip.alt: A stick in the ground casts a shadow; the first and the second marks of the shadow tip lie on a line from E to W, the approximate east-west line; across it runs the noon line from S to N.

atp-watch.alt: Two watches lying flat. Top, north temperate zone: the hour hand points at the sun, and the dashed line midway to the 12 points to N. Bottom, south temperate zone: the 12 points at the sun.

atp-northern-sky.title: Figure 7-11. Northern sky
atp-northern-sky.alt: The night sky: lines lead from the Big Dipper and from Cassiopeia to Polaris, between them; an arrow from Polaris points straight down to the horizon, to the North Pole.

labels.3: 3. Twist one strand around the other counterclockwise.

atp-twisting-fibers.title: Figure A-21. Twisting fibers
atp-twisting-fibers.alt: Two hands twist two strands of fibre, each in its own direction, while the strands are laid up into a cord.

atp-square-knot.title: Figure A-5. Square knot
atp-square-knot.alt: Three steps: the two ends crossed; crossed again; the finished square knot, each end lying beside its own rope.

atp-sheet-bend.title: Figure A-6. Single sheet bend
atp-sheet-bend.alt: Three steps: a bight in the thicker rope; the end of the thinner rope passed through it, around both parts and under itself; the finished knot.

atp-double-sheet-bend.title: Figure A-7. Double sheet bend
atp-double-sheet-bend.alt: Two steps: an extra turn taken around the bight; the finished double sheet bend.

atp-bowline.title: Figure A-8. Bowline knot
atp-bowline.alt: Three steps: a small loop in the standing part with the end coming up through it; the end going around the standing part and back down; the finished loop.

atp-clove-hitch.title: Figure A-15. Clove hitch
atp-clove-hitch.alt: Steps 1–4, in the middle of a rope: two loops made, laid back to back and slipped over a post. Steps 5–6, at the end of a rope: the rope taken around a post twice, its end coming up under itself.

atp-round-turn.title: Figure A-3. Round turn and two half hitches
atp-round-turn.alt: A rope taken around a post and finished with two half hitches around its standing part.

atp-half-hitches.title: Figure A-12. Half hitch and a two half hitch
atp-half-hitches.alt: A: a single half hitch around a pole, in two steps. B: two half hitches around a pole, in three steps.

atp-square-lashing.title: Figure A-18. Square lashing
atp-square-lashing.alt: Four steps of a square lashing of two crossed poles, each with its words: the clove hitch, the turns around both poles, three or four turns, the frapping turns.

labels.1: 1. Start by tying a clove hitch to the vertical spar, just below where the horizontal spar will be.
labels.2: 2. Twist the end of the rope around the verical part of the rope for a clean look, then wrap the rope around the horizontal and vertical spars, binding them together.
labels.3: 3. Continue by wrapping the rope three or four times around the vertical and horizontal spars.
labels.4: 4. Make two or three frapping turns between the spars, around the rope itself. Pull these frapping turns very taut. Finish by tying a clove hitch to the horizontal spar.
